newsitem.title: UK: 'Great Train' thief faces extradition 27 years on.
newsitem.headline: 'Great Train' thief faces extradition 27 years on.

text.p: Ronnie Biggs, Britain's most famous fugitive who fled to Brazil 27 years ago after taking part in a legendary heist known as the "Great Train Robbery", could finally be extradited under a pending new bilateral treaty.

The hold-up captured the country's imagination when a group of men made off with 2.6 million pounds in 1963 -- the equivalent of about 30 million pounds ($50 million) at today's values -- from a Royal Mail train after fixing the track's signals and separating the sections of the train.

The thieves were eventually captured and sent to prison, but Biggs, now 67, escaped after serving just 15 months of a 30-year sentence and settled in Brazil, a popular haven for international fugitives because of its lack of extradition laws.
But with an agreement between Britain and Brazil due to be ratified early next month, Biggs could be forced to surrender to British authorities after so many years in exile.

In an interview with the BBC he said he would not attempt to flee. "I don't think I would run because, number one, I can't afford to. I don't have a current passport to run to another country and I don't think there would be much future in trying to hide out in the boondocks in Brazil somewhere," he said.
"I must admit that it's looking a little bit grim at the moment, but I've been blessed with fantastically good luck over the years and I just hope that luck continues to hold out."
But he added: "In the event of the Brazilian government deciding that I must go back, then go back I shall."

Biggs has infuriated British authorities by flaunting his presence in Brazil over the years, appearing on television to promote his autobiography and living in a flat with a giant Union Jack flag signed by his many visitors.

He was protected by the lack of an extradition treaty and the fact that he had a dependent Brazilian-born son. But his son is now 23 years old and legally independent. He said he hoped he would not be forced to serve out his entire sentence, adding that while he would not go on the run he would fight extradition. He has consulted both British and Brazilian lawyers about his case.
"I'm going to take whatever measures I can here in Brazil to avoid extradition," he said.
